ch56.anchor: This was the nineteenth of the fourth month
ch56.note: The storming of Utsunomiya Castle told here fell on Keiō 4/4/19 (about 11 May 1868) and was the high-water mark of the shogunal remnant’s march north. The victory did not hold: the new government’s main force retook the castle four days later, on the twenty-third, and Hijikata was shot in the foot in the defense. The army then fell back toward Nikkō and, in time, Aizu — the long retreat that carries the rest of the novel.

The “hanging ceiling of Utsunomiya” is a favorite of the street storytellers: the tale that Honda Masazumi, lord of the castle, built a chamber with a ceiling rigged to drop and crush the second shogun, Hidetada, as he lodged there on his way back from Nikkō in 1622. The plot (the Utsunomiya Affair, for which Masazumi was disgraced) is now generally thought a later invention, but it made the castle’s name a byword. Toshizō means that he knows the place only from the theater.

ch56.anchor: the strategic part that Kusunoki Masashige had played in the Kenmu Restoration
ch56.note: Kusunoki Masashige (met in an earlier chapter) held the little mountain fort of Chihaya against a huge army of the Kamakura shogunate in 1333, and by tying it down helped bring on the brief imperial restoration of the Kenmu era. To make Nikkō a “Chihaya” was to gamble that a small force in strong mountains could pin the new government in place and rally the wavering lords — the whole strategy on which this campaign rests.

ch56.anchor: what the art of war calls a focal ground
ch56.note: Kuchi, a “focal ground,” is one of the nine kinds of terrain in Sun Tzu: a junction where several roads meet, so that whoever holds it commands the approaches to a whole region. Utsunomiya, where the northern highway and the Nikkō roads cross, is exactly such a place, which is why Toshizō insists on taking it while Ōtori’s bookish caution misses the point.

An akazonae was a crack unit turned out entirely in red-lacquered armor. The most feared were the red troops of the Takeda house of Kai; after Takeda fell, Ieyasu drafted its veterans into the Ii house of Hikone, whose “Red Regiment” then led his vanguard at Sekigahara and at the Osaka sieges. That the Ii, once his fiercest van, now marched against the Tokugawa under the Emperor’s banner is the irony Arima and Kagawa are turning over.

ch56.anchor: one of the Three Houses of the Tokugawa
ch56.note: The gosanke, the “Three Houses,” were the senior cadet branches of the Tokugawa — Owari, Kii, and Mito — from any of which a shogun could be drawn if the main line failed. Mito, Kagawa’s old domain, was in doctrine the most fiercely loyalist of the three, which is the barb in the narrator’s aside: a Mito man leading the Emperor’s troops against the house he was bred to serve.
